Let me paint you a picture.
You buy a game. A co-op game. A good one. You sit down, excited to play it with your friend. You hit launch. Nothing happens. You hit it again. Still nothing. The EA app flashes for a second and dies.
What followed was 3+ hours of:

Broken system repos blocking every install
Manually editing Linux source files just to get Wine working
Installing ProtonUp-Qt, Lutris, GE-Proton, WineHQ
Switching Proton versions one by one
Digging through Steam logs only to find EA's app crashing silently in the background — every single time

A game from 2018. Not a AAA live-service monster. A simple co-op story game. And it still can't launch because EA decided their mandatory background launcher needs to exist for absolutely no reason.
No other game in my library needed this. Not one.
The game itself? Probably great. Wouldn't know.
EA's launcher? An embarrassment.
Do better. Or get off Steam.

claims.claim: The game features split-screen gameplay throughout the entire experience.

citations.review_text:
It’s a 2-player, co-op-only, linear action-adventure game. It can be played equally well in split-screen or online, as long as you have good comms.
Our playthrough took about 8 hours without rushing, but there are at least two approaches to most situations and two endings, so content-wise it may be worth two playthroughs. We enjoyed most of the action scenes, and there was some humor sprinkled throughout.
The graphics were good and the game runs well, but the environments, outside the many cutscenes, felt empty, too “clean,” and artificial. The voice acting was pretty good, but the music and sound effects were less impressive.
The story is kind of cliché, and the characters didn’t feel relatable to us. We found most “puzzles” to be more of a race between us than an actual challenge, and the few competitive mini-games scattered around felt simplistic and boring.
I was mostly annoyed by the constant co-op action points that sync you with your partner for the next cutscene, as well as the ridiculously easy QTEs, which seemed to exist just to keep you awake between cutscenes.

Day 1

The game starts off pretty cutscene-heavy. It takes a long time before you actually get down to the gameplay. Once it does, though, it’s pretty fun. We were kind of taken aback that the game is split-screen the entire time, so just keep in mind you’re always going to be seeing your partner’s screen. It actually works pretty well for puzzles since you can see what they’re doing.

It’s definitely different from what I’m used to playing. There aren’t really any consequences for failing because you usually just restart at the checkpoint, so it feels like a step above a Telltale game where you’re getting a little more gameplay.

One of my favorite parts was having one person act as the lookout while the other removed the toilet, and all the little puzzles throughout the prison to slowly work toward escaping. Then the game kind of turns itself on its head by having you escape much earlier than I expected. It made me think there was something much bigger going on than just a prison break.

So far, pretty good first impression.

⸻

Day 2

Day two started kind of rough because we ran into a glitch where we couldn’t progress without restarting the checkpoint. We wasted a lot of time trying to figure it out because the game has so many little optional interactions that we thought we had just missed something.

The amount of cutscenes also started getting to me. We just wanted to play the game. I know that’s not really the game’s fault, but this isn’t Metal Gear Solid 4. It felt like every time we’d get going, another long cutscene would pop up.

There was also one mission where you’re not supposed to take damage, and we swear the game eventually just gave us a mercy pass because we kept getting hit.

By this point the story was getting really sappy for me. It wasn’t terrible, but it just wasn’t grabbing me. The game still felt like a Telltale game with just a little more gameplay mixed in. I still liked it overall, but we were already starting to feel like we just wante…

KINDA SPOILER! KINDA!
One of the most depressing endings I have ever seen.
Overall, game is really good. Thumbs up for option to play it split-screen in the same computer.
But still, that ending. Whatever option you choose, you feel like a monster.

citations.review_text:
# A Way Out — Steam Review

Honestly, this game was way more fun than I expected. The best part is that it actually feels like a game made for two people, rather than a normal game with co-op added to it.

The story starts a little slow, but once things get going, it becomes really hard to stop playing. Leo and Vincent have completely different personalities, and playing through their escape together makes the whole experience feel like you're inside a movie.

The gameplay isn't extremely complicated, but that's not really the point. One moment you're sneaking around, the next you're fighting, driving, escaping, or just messing around with random mini-games. Playing with a friend makes even the stupid little moments hilarious.

And that ending... definitely worth playing without spoilers. I genuinely didn't expect things to go the way they did.

It's not a perfect game, and it's fairly short, but as a co-op experience, it's absolutely worth playing with a friend.

**9/10 — Great story, great co-op, and one hell of an ending.**

Would definitely recommend it if you have someone to play with.

One of the best co-op experiences out there! The story, variety of mini-games, and dynamic camera angles keep you hooked until the very end. Unlocking all 14/14 achievements with a friend was a blast!

★★★★★

# A Way Out — a story about escaping, but also about not being alone

There are games you finish and simply close.
You watch the credits, return to your desktop, and go on with the rest of your day as if nothing happened.

And then there are games that end, but somehow stay with you.

*A Way Out* is one of those games.

I started this game expecting a fun co-op experience. Maybe a few hours of action, some jokes between two friends, and an interesting story to follow. And, in a way, that is exactly what I found. But I also found something I wasn't expecting: a story that slowly stops being just about two men trying to escape from prison and becomes a story about trust, friendship, choices, regret, and how some people enter our lives exactly when we need them the most.

The premise seems simple. Two men, Vincent and Leo, completely different from each other, end up in the same place and have to work together to escape.

But what makes *A Way Out* special is that you are never truly alone.

Everything in the game seems to have been built around that idea.

You don't just play *with* someone. You play *because of* someone.

While one character is talking, the other might be doing something completely different. While one is driving, the other is shooting. While one tries to convince someone, the other looks for a way forward. Sometimes, the two of them simply stop to talk, play some four-in-a-row, go fishing, or do something completely irrelevant to the story.

And those irrelevant moments are exactly what make the experience feel so human.

Because life is full of them too.

Not everything has to lead somewhere.

Sometimes you're just sitting next to someone.

And that's enough.

## Prison is only the beginning

The first thing that impressed me about *A Way Out* was how the game manages to turn such a simple situation into something cinematic.

The prison isn't just a setting. It feels like it is suffocating the characters. The corridors, the cells, the guards…

I feel that this game has not aged well. It just never really feels like anything eventful is ever happening and the game gives you very little to do. "Oh great, it's my turn to press the designated button the game is forcing me to press." No options on what you can do or different ways to distract guards or anything. Sometimes you get to keep a lookout while your partner picks up a tool or something or you have to press the designated button with a specific timing.

2/5
This may have been a great game in its day, but now its very boring. There are much better co-op games to choose from in 2026.

A good story-driven game.

The story is definitely the main draw here, especially since cutscenes take up most of your playtime and the game keeps you on a very narrow, linear path regarding where to go and what to do.

It’s highly atmospheric, but the game mechanics and co-op elements aren’t anything special - It Takes Two was definitely more interesting mechanics-wise. Most of the time, you’re on strict rails and just pressing a button here and there. Your available actions are always limited and prompted by the game.

Because of this, experienced gamers might not find it all that engaging. However, it’s ideal for people looking for a gameplay-light, story-rich, and atmospheric experience. As two fairly inexperienced players, we finished it in about 7 hours.

Mild recommendation.
